claim: The glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP1R) is a broadly expressed target of peptide hormones with essential roles in energy and glucose homeostasis.
source: The glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP1R) is a broadly expressed target of peptide hormones with essential roles in energy and glucose homeostasis, as well as of the blockbuster weight-loss drugs semaglutide and liraglutide.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established scientific knowledge about GLP1R function.

claim: GLP1R is a target of the blockbuster weight-loss drugs semaglutide and liraglutide.
source: The glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP1R) is a broadly expressed target of peptide hormones with essential roles in energy and glucose homeostasis, as well as of the blockbuster weight-loss drugs semaglutide and liraglutide.
evidence: This statement references known clinical applications of these drugs.

claim: GLPLight1 is a novel genetically encoded sensor based on engineering of a circularly permuted green fluorescent protein into the human GLP1R.
source: Here, we introduce a novel genetically encoded sensor based on the engineering of a circularly permuted green fluorescent protein into the human GLP1R, named GLPLight1.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly stated in the abstract describing the new tool developed.

claim: GLPLight1 fluorescence signal accurately reports receptor conformational activation in response to pharmacological ligands with high sensitivity (max ΔF/F0=528%).
source: We demonstrate that fluorescence signal from GLPLight1 accurately reports the expected receptor conformational activation in response to pharmacological ligands with high sensitivity (max ΔF/F0=528%) and temporal resolution (τON = 4.7 s).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements reported in the abstract.

claim: GLPLight1 has a temporal resolution of τON = 4.7 s.
source: We demonstrate that fluorescence signal from GLPLight1 accurately reports the expected receptor conformational activation in response to pharmacological ligands with high sensitivity (max ΔF/F0=528%) and temporal resolution (τON = 4.7 s).
evidence: This is a measured kinetic parameter reported in the abstract.

claim: GLPLight1 shows comparable responses to glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) derivatives as observed for the native receptor.
source: We further demonstrated that GLPLight1 shows comparable responses to glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) derivatives as observed for the native receptor.
evidence: This is a finding from comparative experiments stated in the abstract.

claim: A novel photocaged GLP-1 derivative (photo-GLP1) was developed.
source: Using GLPLight1, we established an all-optical assay to characterize a novel photocaged GLP-1 derivative (photo-GLP1) and to demonstrate optical control of GLP1R activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding describing a new chemical tool developed in the study.

claim: Photo-GLP1 enables optical control of GLP1R activation.
source: Using GLPLight1, we established an all-optical assay to characterize a novel photocaged GLP-1 derivative (photo-GLP1) and to demonstrate optical control of GLP1R activation.
evidence: This is a functional demonstration reported in the abstract.

claim: GLP1R is expressed in various parts of the brain, especially in the basolateral amygdala and hypothalamic regions.
source: The glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP1R) is expressed in various parts of the brain, especially in the basolateral amygdala and hypothalamic regions (Alvarez et al., 2005; Cork et al., 2015; Trapp and Brierley, 2022; Turton et al., 1996), as well as broadly outside the central nervous system (Campos et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: GLP1R is expressed broadly outside the central nervous system.
source: The glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP1R) is expressed in various parts of the brain, especially in the basolateral amygdala and hypothalamic regions (Alvarez et al., 2005; Cork et al., 2015; Trapp and Brierley, 2022; Turton et al., 1996), as well as broadly outside the central nervous system (Campos et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) is a peptide fully conserved across mammals.
source: Its endogenous ligand, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), is a peptide, fully conserved across mammals, that carries out both central and endocrine hormonal functions for the control of energy homeostasis (Andersen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: GLP-1 carries out both central and endocrine hormonal functions for the control of energy homeostasis.
source: Its endogenous ligand, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), is a peptide, fully conserved across mammals, that carries out both central and endocrine hormonal functions for the control of energy homeostasis (Andersen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: GLP-1 is produced mainly by preproglucagon (PPG) neurons principally located in the nucleus of the solitary tract of the brain.
source: GLP-1 is produced mainly by two cell types: preproglucagon (PPG) neurons principally located in the nucleus of the solitary tract of the brain (Trapp and Brierley, 2022; Turton et al., 1996), and enterocrine cells (ECs) located in the gut (Trapp and Brierley, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: GLP-1 is produced mainly by enterocrine cells (ECs) located in the gut.
source: GLP-1 is produced mainly by two cell types: preproglucagon (PPG) neurons principally located in the nucleus of the solitary tract of the brain (Trapp and Brierley, 2022; Turton et al., 1996), and enterocrine cells (ECs) located in the gut (Trapp and Brierley, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: Upon ingestion of a meal, GLP-1 is rapidly released along with gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP) from the gut into the bloodstream.
source: Upon ingestion of a meal, GLP-1 is rapidly released along with gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP) from the gut into the bloodstream where it targets β-cells of the pancreas and stimulates the production and secretion of insulin under hyperglycemic conditions (Andersen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: GLP-1 targets β-cells of the pancreas and stimulates the production and secretion of insulin under hyperglycemic conditions.
source: Upon ingestion of a meal, GLP-1 is rapidly released along with gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP) from the gut into the bloodstream where it targets β-cells of the pancreas and stimulates the production and secretion of insulin under hyperglycemic conditions (Andersen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: The incretin effect is impaired in metabolic disorders, such as type 2 diabetes mellitus.
source: This phenomenon, known as the 'incretin effect' (Nauck and Meier, 2018), is impaired in metabolic disorders, such as type 2 diabetes mellitus (Holst et al., 2009), making GLP-1 signaling an attractive therapeutic target for the treatment of these disorders.
evidence: This claim is supported by literature citations.

claim: Central GLP-1 plays central neuroprotective roles.
source: In addition to its role in controlling satiety and food intake, central GLP-1 has also been shown to play central neuroprotective roles (Hölscher, 2022), illustrating its multifaceted role in human physiology.
evidence: This claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP1RAs) have been used for decades for the treatment of type 2 diabetes.
source: The human GLP1R (hmGLP1R) is a prime target for drug screening and drug development efforts, since GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP1RAs) have been used for decades for the treatment of type 2 diabetes and have more recently become some of the most effective and widely used weight-loss drugs (Shah and Vella, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: GLP-1 receptor agonists have more recently become some of the most effective and widely used weight-loss drugs.
source: The human GLP1R (hmGLP1R) is a prime target for drug screening and drug development efforts, since GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP1RAs) have been used for decades for the treatment of type 2 diabetes and have more recently become some of the most effective and widely used weight-loss drugs (Shah and Vella, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a literature citation.

claim: The initial sensor prototype had poor surface expression and a very small fluorescence response (ΔF/F0=39%) upon addition of 10 µM GLP-1.
source: This initial sensor prototype had poor surface expression and a very small fluorescence response upon addition of a saturating concentration (10 µM) of GLP-1 (ΔF/F0=39%, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a measured result from sensor development experiments, with reference to a figure.

claim: Removal of the endogenous GLP1R N-terminal secretory sequence (amino acids 1–23) improved the membrane expression and the fluorescence response to GLP-1 (ΔF/F0=107%).
source: Removal of the endogenous GLP1R N-terminal secretory sequence (amino acids 1–23) from this construct improved the membrane expression and the fluorescence response to GLP-1 (ΔF/F0=107%, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a measured result from sensor optimization experiments, with reference to a figure.

claim: The L260K mutation more than doubled the dynamic range of the sensor (ΔF/F0=180%).
source: From this screening we identified one beneficial mutation (L260K) that more than doubled the dynamic range of the sensor (ΔF/F0=180%, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a measured result from mutagenesis screening, with reference to a figure.

claim: The K336Y and T343N mutations resulted in a sensor variant with ΔF/F0 of about 341%.
source: This small-scale screening led us to identification of a new variant (containing the mutations K336Y and T343N) with ΔF/F0 of about 341% (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c–d).
evidence: This is a measured result from mutagenesis screening, with reference to figures.

claim: The final GLPLight1 sensor variant showed a 528% maximal fluorescence response upon GLP-1 binding.
source: The resulting sensor variant showed good membrane expression and a 528% maximal fluorescence response upon GLP-1 binding (Figure 1b–c, Figure 1—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: This is a measured result for the final sensor, with reference to figures.

claim: GLPLight-ctr is a control variant carrying mutations (L141A, N300A, and E387A) that abolished the fluorescent response to GLP-1 application.
source: We screened a panel of 14 single point mutations and identified a combination of 3 mutations (L141A, N300A, and E387A) that abolished the fluorescent response to GLP-1 application while showing a good membrane expression of the sensor (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a–c).
evidence: This is a result from mutagenesis screening for a control variant, with reference to figures.

claim: GLPLight1 expressed in primary cortical neurons showed a maximal response of 456% to GLP-1 application (10 µM).
source: Two weeks post-transduction, GLPLight1 was well expressed on the neuronal membrane and showed a maximal response of 456% to GLP-1 application (10 µM) (Figure 1b–c).
evidence: This is a measured result in neurons, with reference to a figure.

claim: GLPLight1 has a peak excitation around 500 nm and peak emission around 512 nm.
source: The fluorescence spectra were similar to those of previously described green GPCR-sensors (Duffet et al., 2022a; Sun et al., 2018), and showed a peak excitation around 500 nm, peak emission around 512 nm, and an isosbestic point at around 425 nm (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a measured spectral property, with reference to a figure and comparison to literature.

claim: GLPLight1 has an isosbestic point at around 425 nm.
source: The fluorescence spectra were similar to those of previously described green GPCR-sensors (Duffet et al., 2022a; Sun et al., 2018), and showed a peak excitation around 500 nm, peak emission around 512 nm, and an isosbestic point at around 425 nm (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a measured spectral property, with reference to a figure.

claim: The coupling of GLPLight1 to all tested signaling partners (miniGs, miniGq, miniGi, β-arrestin-2, miniG12) was significantly reduced compared to WT GLP1R.
source: In comparison to WT GLP1R, the coupling of GLPLight1 to all tested signaling partners was significantly reduced (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–j).
evidence: This is a measured result from signaling assays, with reference to figures.

claim: WT GLP1R showed an EC50 of 8.0 pM for eliciting intracellular cAMP increases.
source: This revealed that the WT GLP1R showed could potently elicit intracellular cAMP increases with an EC50 of 8.0 pM whereas no such increase was observed for GLPLight1 even at the highest GLP-1 concentrations tested (100 nM, Figure 1—figure supplement 3k).
evidence: This is a measured EC50 value from cAMP assays, with reference to a figure.

claim: GLPLight1 showed no intracellular cAMP increase even at 100 nM GLP-1.
source: This revealed that the WT GLP1R showed could potently elicit intracellular cAMP increases with an EC50 of 8.0 pM whereas no such increase was observed for GLPLight1 even at the highest GLP-1 concentrations tested (100 nM, Figure 1—figure supplement 3k).
evidence: This is a measured result from cAMP assays, with reference to a figure.

claim: GLP1R effectively recruits miniGs proteins with an EC50 of 3.8 nM.
source: We also performed a titration of GLP-1-induced recruitment of miniGs protein where we could show that GLP1R effectively recruits miniGs proteins with an EC50 of 3.8 nM (Figure 1—figure supplement 3l).
evidence: This is a measured EC50 value from miniGs recruitment assays, with reference to a figure.

claim: GLPLight1 is unlikely to couple with endogenous intracellular signaling pathways.
source: These results indicate that GLPLight1 is unlikely to couple with endogenous intracellular signaling pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cAMP and G protein coupling data.

claim: Exendin-9 (Ex-9) could partially reverse the GLPLight1 signal to 42% of the maximal GLP-1 response within less than 5 min in vitro.
source: Ex-9 could partially reverse the signal to 42% of the maximal GLP-1 response, within less than 5 min in vitro (Figure 2a–b).
evidence: This is a measured result from antagonist competition experiments, with reference to figures.

claim: GLPLight1 responded to liraglutide and semaglutide with almost maximal activation, on par with GLP1.
source: As expected, GLPLight1 responded to both GLP1RAs with almost maximal activation, on par with GLP1 (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a measured result from drug testing experiments, with reference to a figure.

claim: GLPLight1 did not respond with any detectable increase in fluorescence to GLP-2.
source: While the sensor did not respond with any detectable increase in fluorescence to GLP-2, it responded to glucagon with a ΔF/F0 of 324% (61% of maximal response to GLP-1).
evidence: This is a measured result from peptide specificity testing.

claim: GLPLight1 responded to glucagon with a ΔF/F0 of 324% (61% of maximal response to GLP-1).
source: While the sensor did not respond with any detectable increase in fluorescence to GLP-2, it responded to glucagon with a ΔF/F0 of 324% (61% of maximal response to GLP-1).
evidence: This is a measured result from peptide specificity testing.

claim: GLPLight1 had a 94-fold higher affinity for GLP-1 compared to glucagon (EC50=28 nM for GLP-1, EC50=2.6 µM for glucagon).
source: To further characterize the sensitivity of GLPLight1 to its two endogenous agonists, we performed titrations of GLP-1 and glucagon in HEK293T cells and determined that GLPLight1 had a 94-fold higher affinity for GLP-1 compared to glucagon (EC50=28 nM for GLP-1, EC50=2.6 µM for glucagon), in agreement with previously reported results employing a downstream cAMP readout (Runge et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a measured result from dose-response experiments, with comparison to literature.

claim: The affinity of GLP-1 measured in primary neurons (EC50=9.3 nM) was comparable to the one in HEK cells.
source: Furthermore, the affinity of GLP-1 measured in primary neurons (EC50=9.3 nM) was comparable to the one in HEK cells (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a measured result comparing sensor performance in different cell types, with reference to a figure.

claim: GLPLight1 did not respond to a panel of other endogenous class B1 GPCR peptide ligands (GIP, CRF, PTH, PACAP, VIP) tested at 1.0 µM.
source: Additionally, GLPLight1 did not respond to a panel of other endogenous class B1 GPCR peptide ligands that were tested at high concentration (1.0 µM), including GIP, CRF, PTH, PACAP, or VIP.
evidence: This is a measured result from peptide specificity testing.

claim: The H1A mutant of GLP-1 showed a significant reduction of Emax (56%) and EC50 (1300 nM) compared to WT GLP-1.
source: In agreement with these results, we observed a significant reduction of Emax and EC50 for H1A (56% and 1300 nM, respectively) (Table 1, Entry a) and G4A (14% and 993 nM, respectively) (Table 1, Entry c), compared to WT GLP-1 using GLP1Light as a readout.
evidence: This is a measured result from alanine scanning experiments, with reference to a table.

claim: The G4A mutant of GLP-1 showed a significant reduction of Emax (14%) and EC50 (993 nM) compared to WT GLP-1.
source: In agreement with these results, we observed a significant reduction of Emax and EC50 for H1A (56% and 1300 nM, respectively) (Table 1, Entry a) and G4A (14% and 993 nM, respectively) (Table 1, Entry c), compared to WT GLP-1 using GLP1Light as a readout.
evidence: This is a measured result from alanine scanning experiments, with reference to a table.

claim: The E3A mutant of GLP-1 showed an Emax of 96% and EC50 of 757 nM compared to WT GLP-1.
source: Here, we determined an Emax of 96% compared to WT GLP-1 (Table 1, Entry b), as well as a reduced EC50 (757 nM) for E3A, which is in agreement with the literature (Manandhar and Ahn, 2015; Table 1).
evidence: This is a measured result from alanine scanning experiments, with reference to a table and literature.

claim: The T5A mutant of GLP-1 showed the highest Emax (100%) and EC50 (188 nM) of all alanine mutants investigated.
source: Accordingly, our experiments with GLPLight1 T5A showed the highest Emax (100%) and EC50 (188 nM) (Table 1, Entry d) of all alanine mutants investigated herein.
evidence: This is a measured result from alanine scanning experiments, with reference to a table.

claim: The response to GLP-1 of sensor-expressing cells cultured in the presence of GLUTag cells was significantly lower than that of cells cultured in their absence.
source: We observed that the response to GLP-1 of sensor-expressing cells cultured in the presence of GLUTag cells was significantly lower than that of cells cultured in their absence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a measured result from co-culture experiments, with reference to a figure.

claim: GLPLight1 was partially pre-activated by endogenous GLP-1 secreted by GLUTag cells.
source: These results indicate that GLPLight1 was partially pre-activated by endogenous GLP-1 secreted by the ECs present in the dish.
evidence: This is an inference based on the co-culture experiment results.

claim: Photo-GLP1 was obtained in 5% overall yield with >95% purity after RP-HPLC purification.
source: Cleavage of the resulting photocaged peptide from the resin followed by RP-HPLC purification successfully provided photo-GLP1 in 5% overall yield with >95% purity.
evidence: This is a measured result from peptide synthesis.

claim: LCMS and UHPLC analysis demonstrated complete uncaging of photo-GLP1 to afford WT GLP-1 after 20 min irradiation with LED light (λ=370 nm, 0.64 mW/mm2).
source: Subsequent LCMS and UHPLC analysis demonstrated complete uncaging of photo-GLP1 to afford WT GLP-1, confirmed by co-injection of a standard sample of WT GLP-1 (80 µM in HBSS) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a measured result from analytical chemistry experiments, with reference to a figure.

claim: Application of photo-GLP1 by itself failed to trigger any response from GLPLight1.
source: Application of photo-GLP1 by itself failed to trigger any response from GLPLight1, indicating a lack of functional activity in the absence of UV light (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is a measured result from uncaging experiments, with reference to a figure.

claim: After photo-GLP1 was added to the bath, the fluorescence of GLPLight1 visibly increased upon 10 s of UV light exposure.
source: On the contrary, after photo-GLP1 was added to the bath, the fluorescence of GLPLight1 visibly increased upon 10 s of UV light exposure, indicating that GLP-1 could successfully be uncaged and activated the sensor on the cells.
evidence: This is a measured result from uncaging experiments.

claim: The maximal uncaging duration tested (100 s) triggered approximately 30% of the maximal response of the sensor.
source: Higher durations of UV light exposure led to a higher degree of GLPLight1 responses, and the maximal uncaging duration tested (100 s) triggered approximately 30% of the maximal response of the sensor, as assessed in the same assay by bath application of a saturating GLP-1 concentration (10 µM) (Figure 3b–c).
evidence: This is a measured result from uncaging experiments, with reference to figures.

claim: Pre-treatment of the cells with the GLP1R antagonist Ex-9 significantly blunted the sensor response evoked by the optical uncaging (100 s).
source: Furthermore, pre-treatment of the cells with the GLP1R antagonist Ex-9 significantly blunted the sensor response evoked by the optical uncaging (100 s) (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is a measured result from antagonist control experiments, with reference to figures.

claim: The sensor response exhibited an approximate 14-fold reduction in the speed of activation in the presence of photo-GLP1 (τON without photo-GLP1=4.7 s; τON with photo-GLP1=68.1 s).
source: The sensor response was strikingly different in the two conditions, and exhibited an approximate 14-fold reduction in the speed of activation in the presence of photo-GLP1 (τON without photo-GLP1=4.7 s; τON with photo-GLP1=68.1 s; Figure 3d–e).
evidence: This is a measured result from kinetic experiments, with reference to figures.

claim: Photo-GLP1, in the dark, can affect the kinetics of GLP1R activation, likely mediated by its binding to the receptor extracellular domain (ECD).
source: These results indicate that photo-GLP1, in the dark (i.e. with an intact photocage), can affect the kinetics of GLP1R activation, and this is likely mediated by its binding to the receptor extracellular domain (ECD), which competes for the functionally active GLP-1.
evidence: This is an inference based on kinetic data and knowledge of receptor binding mechanisms.

claim: GLPLight1 shows a fluorescent response in all three uncaged areas, while its fluorescence remained unaltered throughout the rest of the FOV.
source: GLPLight1 shows a fluorescent response in all three uncaged areas, while its fluorescence remained unaltered throughout the rest of the FOV, indicating high spatial localization of the response to GLP-1 (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is a measured result from spatial uncaging experiments, with reference to a figure.

claim: Application of UV light led to localized activation of GLPLight1 that was limited to a portion of the cell membrane and did not spread to neighboring cells.
source: In this case, the application of UV light led to localized activation of GLPLight1 that was limited to a portion of the cell membrane and did not spread to neighboring cells (Figure 3h).
evidence: This is a measured result from sub-cellular uncaging experiments, with reference to a figure.

claim: As a result of uncaging, the signal from the cAMP sensor increased visibly and significantly only in the cell directly underneath the uncaged area.
source: As a result of uncaging, the signal from the cAMP sensor increased visibly and significantly only in the cell directly underneath the uncaged area (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a measured result from cAMP sensor experiments with photo-GLP1 uncaging, with reference to a figure.

claim: The same uncaging protocol applied in the absence of photo-GLP1 on the cells failed to trigger any response from the cAMP sensor.
source: The same uncaging protocol applied in the absence of photo-GLP1 on the cells failed to trigger any response from the cAMP sensor , indicating that the sensor signals reliably reported intracellular cAMP signaling triggered by uncaged GLP-1.
evidence: This is a measured result from control experiments.

claim: Ligand-induced conformational activation of the hmGLP1R occurs on slower timescales compared to the reported kinetics of other similarly built GPCR sensors.
source: Using this new probe, we found that ligand-induced conformational activation of the hmGLP1R occurs on slower timescales compared to the reported kinetics of other similarly built GPCR sensors (Labouesse and Patriarchi, 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from kinetic measurements compared to literature.

claim: GLP1R belongs to class B1 GPCRs characterized by a distinct ligand-binding mechanism that involved initial ligand 'capture' by the receptor's ECD, followed by ligand insertion into the receptor binding pocket.
source: This new insight is not surprising given that previously developed sensors were built from class A GPCRs (Labouesse and Patriarchi, 2021), while GLP1R belongs to a different class of GPCRs (class B1) that is characterized by a distinct ligand-binding mechanism that involved initial ligand 'capture' by the receptor's ECD, followed by ligand insertion into the receptor binding pocket for initiating the transduction of signaling (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about GPCR classification and binding mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: Other previously characterized class A GPCR-based neuropeptide biosensors showed sub-second activation kinetics.
source: As a reference, other previously characterized class A GPCR-based neuropeptide biosensors showed sub-second activation kinetics (Duffet et al., 2022a; Ino et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a comparison to literature on other sensors.

claim: The apparent EC50 of GLPLight1 fluorescence response to GLP-1 is very similar to that measured for miniGs recruitment to the hmGLP1R.
source: The apparent EC50 of GLPLight1 fluorescence response to GLP-1 is very similar to that measured for miniGs recruitment to the hmGLP1R, while it is approximately three orders of magnitude lower than that of the cAMP response downstream of hmGLP1R.
evidence: This is a comparison of measured EC50 values from different assays.

claim: The apparent EC50 of GLPLight1 fluorescence response to GLP-1 is approximately three orders of magnitude lower than that of the cAMP response downstream of hmGLP1R.
source: The apparent EC50 of GLPLight1 fluorescence response to GLP-1 is very similar to that measured for miniGs recruitment to the hmGLP1R, while it is approximately three orders of magnitude lower than that of the cAMP response downstream of hmGLP1R.
evidence: This is a comparison of measured EC50 values from different assays.

claim: Under physiological conditions GLP-1 might elicit different functional responses based on the location of its action and on the spatial concentration gradients on target cells/tissues.
source: This raises the interesting possibility that under physiological conditions GLP-1 might elicit different functional responses based on the location of its action and on the spatial concentration gradients on target cells/tissues.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the EC50 discrepancy observations.

claim: The characteristics of GLPLight1 appear not suitable to detect the concentration range achieved by GLP-1 in the periphery through endocrine signaling (picomolar levels).
source: Given that GLPLight1 produces a fluorescence readout that is more representative in terms of sensitivity to that measured by direct recruitment of miniGs proteins to the hmGLP1R, the characteristics of this sensor appear not suitable to detect the concentration range achieved by GLP-1 in the periphery through endocrine signaling (picomolar levels).
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured sensitivity of the sensor.

claim: Under specific circumstances, for example in specific brain areas or in close proximity to enteroendocrine cells in the gut, levels of GLP-1 release might reach high-enough levels that could be detected by GLPLight1.
source: Nevertheless, it is conceivable that under specific circumstances, for example in specific brain areas or in close proximity to enteroendocrine cells in the gut, levels of GLP-1 release might reach high-enough levels that could be detected by GLPLight1.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications of the sensor.

claim: The photoswitchable GLP-1 LirAzo was recently used to optically control insulin secretion and cell survival.
source: Optical tools to selectively activate GLP1R could contribute to mechanistic studies (Chen et al., 2022; Frank et al., 2018), and the photoswitchable GLP-1 LirAzo was recently used to optically control insulin secretion and cell survival (Broichhagen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a reference to prior work in the literature.

claim: Photo-GLP1 releases native GLP-1 upon optical uncaging.
source: As opposed to photoswitchable peptides, in which the side chain or part of the peptide backbone is replaced by a photoswitchable moiety such as an azobenzene, photo-GLP1 releases native GLP-1 upon optical uncaging.
evidence: This is a description of the mechanism of photo-GLP1.

claim: A drawback of a photocaging strategy is that it is an irreversible transformation, unlike photoswitchable derivatives.
source: A drawback of a photocaging strategy, on the other hand, is that it is an irreversible transformation, unlike photoswitchable derivatives.
evidence: This is a general statement about photocaging chemistry.

claim: The spatial spread of GLP1R activation in response to GLP-1 release can be localized to single-cells or even sub-cellular domains.
source: By deploying GLPLight1 and photo-GLP1 in concert in an all-optical assay, we determined that the spatial spread of GLP1R activation in response to GLP-1 release can be localized to single-cells or even sub-cellular domains.
evidence: This is a finding from spatial uncaging experiments.

claim: Photo-GLP1 might still be susceptible to DPPIV-mediated degradation when used in in vivo applications.
source: Since we photocaged native GLP1, it is important to note that the photo-GLP1 might still be susceptible to DPPIV-mediated degradation when used in in vivo applications.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential limitations based on knowledge of GLP-1 degradation.

claim: DPPIV levels in the brain are significantly lower than in peripheral organs.
source: We envisage that our photo-GLP1 will nonetheless find applications in neurobiological in vivo studies in brain tissue, as DPPIV levels in the brain are significantly lower than in peripheral organs.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about DPPIV distribution.
